statement: A rectangular pool measures 12 m by 5 m. A path 1 m wide runs all the way around the outside of the pool. What is the area of the path, in square metres?

choices.misconception: I added 1 m to the length and to the width instead of 2 m, so I worked out $13 \times 6 - 60 = 18$.
I multiplied the pool's perimeter, 34 m, by the 1 m width and forgot the four corner squares of the path.
I multiplied the outer perimeter, 42 m, by the 1 m width, which counts each corner square twice.
I found the area of the whole outer rectangle, $14 \times 7$, and forgot to take away the pool.

hints: Sketch the pool with the path around it and label the outer measurements.
Draw the diagram: the path is the big outer rectangle minus the pool. Work out how much the path adds to each side length, remembering that it sits on both sides.
The outer rectangle is 14 m by 7 m, because the path adds 1 m at each end. Subtract the pool's $12 \times 5$.

solutions.reliable: The path adds 1 m at both ends of each side, so the outer rectangle is $12 + 2 = 14$ m by $5 + 2 = 7$ m, with area $14 \times 7 = 98$ square metres. The pool covers $12 \times 5 = 60$ square metres. The path is $98 - 60 = 38$ square metres. The transferable idea: a quick sketch with the numbers written on it shows that the path sticks out past the pool at both ends.
solutions.elegant: Split the path into pieces: two long strips $12 \times 1$, two short strips $5 \times 1$ and four $1 \times 1$ corner squares. That is $24 + 10 + 4 = 38$, and the sketch makes the four corners impossible to forget.

whyOnTest: Drawing the path around the pool exposes the corner squares, which is exactly where most mental answers go wrong.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
